articles.title: ENAM abre inscrições para exame obrigatório para quem quer ser juiz | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidatos terão que passar no ENAM antes de disputarem concursos para cargos de juiz na Justiça Federal, Estadual, Trabalhista e Militar.
articles.summary: Candidatos precisam ser aprovados no exame antes de disputar concursos para a magistratura na Justiça Federal, Estadual, Trabalhista e Militar.
articles.body:
Inscritos para o Exame Nacional da Magistratura (ENAM) se encaminham para local de prova, no DF — Foto: TV Globo/Reprodução

As inscrições para o Exame Nacional da Magistratura (ENAM) , prova em que os candidatos precisam ser aprovados antes de prestar concursos para cargos de juiz no país, já estão abertas.

Neste ano, o exame será realizado em 29 de novembro, em todas as capitais brasileiras. As inscrições vão até 24 de setembro, pelo site da Fundação Getulio Vargas ( FGV ), banca organizadora do exame.

A taxa de inscrição é de R$ 120 e deve ser paga até 25 de setembro. Candidatos com renda igual ou inferior ao limite de isenção do Imposto de Renda, inscritos no CadÚnico ou doadores de medula óssea podem solicitar a isenção da taxa.

A prova terá 80 questões sobre direito constitucional, direito administrativo, noções gerais do direito e formação humanística, direitos humanos, direito processual civil, direito civil, direito empresarial e direito penal.

O edital foi regulamentado e organizado pela Escola Nacional de Formação e Aperfeiçoamento de Magistrados (Enfam). A banca responsável pela aplicação do exame é a Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV).

A aprovação no exame é obrigatória para quem pretende participar de concursos para a magistratura promovidos por tribunais regionais federais, tribunais do trabalho, tribunais militares e tribunais dos estados, além do Distrito Federal e dos Territórios.

A medida foi aprovada em novembro de 2023 pelo Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ). A intenção é uniformizar o nível de conhecimento dos candidatos à magistratura, sem retirar a competência dos tribunais de realizarem seus próprios concursos, segundo o ministro Luís Roberto Barroso , presidente do CNJ na época.

Atualmente, a Constituição estabelece que a carreira no Poder Judiciário começa no cargo de juiz substituto, na primeira instância da Justiça.

O cargo é preenchido por concurso público de provas e títulos, com a participação da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil (OAB) em todas as fases.

Para concorrer, o candidato deve ser bacharel em Direito e ter, no mínimo, três anos de atividade jurídica. Com o ENAM, também passa a ser necessário ter sido aprovado no exame nacional. A prova será realizada pelo menos uma vez por ano, de forma simultânea.

Para ser aprovado no ENAM, o candidato deverá acertar 56 das 80 questões, o equivalente a 70% da prova.

Para pessoas autodeclaradas negras, indígenas, quilombolas ou com deficiência, o mínimo é de 40 acertos, ou 50% da prova.

ter nacionalidade brasileira, nata ou naturalizada, ou ser português com direitos amparados pelo Decreto nº 70.391/1972;

ter concluído o curso de graduação em Direito, em instituição pública ou particular reconhecida pelo Ministério da Educação ( MEC ), até o início das inscrições;

estar quite com o serviço militar, no caso de candidato do sexo masculino;

estar quite com as obrigações eleitorais.

A prova terá duração de cinco horas, das 13h às 18h, no horário de Brasília. Os portões serão fechados às 12h30. O gabarito oficial preliminar será divulgado em 1º de dezembro , no site do exame.

Haverá possibilidade de apresentar recursos contra o gabarito preliminar e contra a aplicação da prova. (veja cronograma completo abaixo)

O resultado definitivo da prova objetiva deve ser publicado em 29 de janeiro de 2027. A homologação do resultado final está prevista para 5 de fevereiro de 2027. A certificação de habilitação deverá ocorrer em até 30 dias após a homologação, ou seja, até 7 de março de 2027.

O certificado terá validade de dois anos, podendo ser prorrogado uma única vez, por igual período, contado da data de sua emissão.

O exame terá caráter exclusivamente eliminatório. No dia da prova, será obrigatório apresentar documento de identidade original com foto e levar caneta esferográfica azul ou preta, de material transparente.

Os candidatos deverão permanecer na sala por, no mínimo, três horas e só poderão levar o caderno de questões nos últimos 30 minutos de prova.

Será proibido consultar livros, códigos, legislação, súmulas e anotações, assim como utilizar aparelhos eletrônicos ou manter comunicação com outros candidatos.

articles.title: Cachorrinha presa em fenda por 5 dias é resgatada no Interior do RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Batizada de Josi, a cadelinha desapareceu no sábado (12). Entre a segunda (14) e a quarta-feira (16), foram três dias de tentativas de resgate até que o animal pudesse ser salvo.
articles.summary: Batizada de Josi, a cadelinha desapareceu no sábado (12). Entre a segunda (14) e a quarta-feira (16), foram três dias de tentativas de resgate até que a canina pudesse ser salva.
articles.body:
Uma operação de resgate que mobilizou ONGs da causa animal e a prefeitura de Camaquã resultou no resgate da cadela Josi, que estava presa por cinco dias em uma fenda no interior do município da região Sul do RS.

O desaparecimento de Josi, cujo uivo, choro e latido era possível de ser ouvido por meio da fenda na pedra , aconteceu no sábado (12). A Associação Protetora dos Animais de Rua (Arca) acionou a prefeitura de Camaquã em busca de equipamentos que auxiliassem no resgate e salvamento.

“A primeira tentativa da ONG de resgatar foi na segunda-feira (14), com os bombeiros. Sem sucesso. Ela estava na rocha da fenda, da pedra, e não tínhamos material suficiente. Deixamos para terça-feira (15), mas não tínhamos muito recurso, os bombeiros não conseguiram também. Aí na quarta (16), conseguimos que a prefeitura liberasse uma retroescavadeira”, relata Sabrina Lemes, que atua na ONG.

Mesmo com a retroescavadeira, ainda havia dificuldade para chegar ao ponto onde Josi estava presa. Tentativas de quebrar a pedra foram frustradas, então a equipe passou a cavar ao redor do local.

“Quando o pessoal da pedreira, que entende de pedras, chegou, clareou um pouco as ideias. Começamos a cavar por volta, no barranco. Ela tinha que ter entrado em algum lugar. E foi indo, foi indo, até que deu certo”, lembra Sabrina.

Segundo ela, foram cinco dias entre o desaparecimento da cadelinha Josi ser constatado e conseguir ser retirada da fenda na rocha.

“Ela já estava magrinha. Saiu faceira. Foi muito emocionante ver que o maquinista não desistiu e disse que enquanto a gente estivesse lá, ele ia ficar também”, conta.

articles.title: "Forcing events on underage kids": Candace Owens calls out Erika Kirk and TPUSA school event after 500-plus students reportedly attend Nampa gathering
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Candace Owens has raised questions over a Turning Point USA event at Nampa Christian School after images showed hundreds of students gathered inside a.
articles.body: Candace Owens has raised questions over a Turning Point USA event at Nampa Christian School after images showed hundreds of students gathered inside a school gym. Owens claimed students were required to attend the event and that parents could not join them. The posts quickly drew a response online, turning the school gathering into a wider debate over youth political outreach and Charlie Kirk’s legacy.Candace Owens questions TPUSA event at Nampa Christian SchoolThe controversy began after posts from the event circulated on social media. The photos show a large group of students seated inside a gymnasium, while another image shows a student speaking from a stage carrying Club America branding.Owens responded to a post celebrating the turnout and questioned whether students had a choice about attending. She wrote:“The students were forced to attend this event as a school assembly. They could not opt out.The parents were informed they were not allowed to attend alongside with them.It is insane to me that you have administrations forcing events on underage kids and then are trying to spin it to the public as successful club growth.”The claim about compulsory attendance came from Owens, rather than from the school or TPUSA in the material reviewed for this article. Nampa Christian Schools’ official calendar confirms the school was operating its regular schedule on Sept. 18, although the calendar does not list the Club America gathering.Turning Point USA describes Club America as its high school student movement and says it has more than 1,200 student-led chapters. The organisation says the programme is designed to encourage students to engage in activism and promote what it describes as freedom-loving American values.Club America post celebrates 500-plus students and Erika Kirk appearanceThe images also show a post from Nikkelle Hudak-Cardoso celebrating the event and highlighting the reported turnout. Her post stated:“500+ OUTSTANDING high school students attended the @TPUSA ClubAmerica Tour Stop at Nampa Christian School this morning! 🔥@MrsErikaKirk delivered a powerful message to this generation of America First leaders. The future is bright! 🇺🇸”The event appears to fit into TPUSA’s broader effort to expand its youth presence. The organisation has publicly promoted student programmes and Club America chapters as part of its work with high school students.The posts also prompted another social media response defending the event and comparing it with Charlie Kirk’s previous outreach to schools. The account Cinema Shogun wrote:“TPUSA is doing school events just like Charlie Kirk did when he was alive.Candace Owens is only upset because she’s not included.While TPUSA is carrying on Charlie’s legacy and having a positive impact on the youth...Candace Owens is stuck in her basement pandering to a low IQ audience of deranged ding bats with no future ahead of them.Thats why she’s mad.”The final post is an individual’s characterization of Owens and does not establish why she objected to the event. TPUSA has said its current programmes are intended to continue aspects of Kirk’s political organising and student outreach. Its official materials also describe Erika Kirk as part of the organisation’s current leadership and programming.At the centre of the dispute is therefore a straightforward but unresolved question: what role should political organisations play inside schools, and how much choice should students and parents have when such events take place? The available posts offer sharply different accounts, while the school’s public calendar does not independently settle the claims about attendance or parental access.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bulgaria released 61 Griffon Vultures after they vanished for 60 years, and 10 years later, 42 chicks had fledged in the wild
articles.summary: Europe News: Bulgaria’s Griffon Vulture population has returned to Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park after more than 60 years without breeding there. Between 2010 and .
articles.body: Bulgaria’s Griffon Vulture population has returned to Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park after more than 60 years without breeding there. Between 2010 and 2020, conservationists released 61 rehabilitated and captive-bred Griffon Vultures from Spain, France and European zoos as part of a long-term reintroduction programme. The effort eventually led to successful breeding in the wild, with 42 chicks fledging between 2015 and 2020. The comeback also established a local population of around 55–70 Griffon Vultures by 2020. Sustained monitoring, supplementary feeding and carefully managed releases helped restore a species that had disappeared as a breeding bird from the area.Why did Bulgaria reintroduce Griffon Vultures after 60 yearsAccording to the study published in PubMed, titled ‘Results of the re-introduction of the Griffon Vulture (Gyps fulvus) in Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park, Bulgaria – completion of the establishing phase 2010–2020’, the Griffon Vulture was once widespread across Bulgaria and was reported as numerous until the 1940s. In Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park, researchers found evidence that the species had nested at seven sites until around the 1950s. It later declined and became locally extinct as a breeding species around 1970. The study identifies poison baits used to control mammalian predators as a major reason for the decline.The reintroduction programme was developed after Vrachanski Balkan was identified as suitable because of its extensive inland cliffs, historical presence of Griffon Vultures and the capacity for local conservation management. Preparatory work included field surveys, test feeding and a viability study. The practical reintroduction began in 2010, when the first group of Griffon Vultures imported from Spain was released.Bulgaria released 61 Griffon Vultures from European zoos and centresThe released vultures were either wild-born birds from rehabilitation centres in Spain and France or captive-bred birds from European zoos. Juveniles, adults and immature birds were used. They were first kept in an adaptation aviary before being soft-released using a method developed in France.The researchers recorded 61 released vultures across the 2010–2020 reintroduction programme. The birds were individually marked with metal rings, PVC rings and wing tags so they could be identified and monitored. A supplementary feeding site was also established near the release area, with food provided at least twice a week. The feeding programme used livestock carcasses, including sheep, cattle, horses and pigs, as well as slaughter offal.42 Griffon Vulture chicks fledged in the wild by 2020The species took several years to breed. Researchers first observed breeding behaviour in the wild in 2013. In 2015, five territorial pairs were confirmed, and the first chick successfully fledged in the wild. The study notes that this was the first successfully fledged wild-born Griffon Vulture recorded among all active Griffon Vulture release sites in Bulgaria at that time.Breeding then increased during the following years. The study recorded four fledglings in 2016, six in 2017 and nine in 2018. In 2019, the number rose to 12 fledglings; the population was affected by a large-scale poisoning incident. In 2020, 18 territorial pairs were recorded, with 14 breeding pairs producing seven successful fledglings. Altogether, 42 chicks successfully fledged in the wild between 2015 and 2020.Griffon Vulture population reached 70 birdsBy December 2020, the Griffon Vultures regularly present in Vrachanski Balkan Nature Park numbered about 55–70 individuals. The population included around 20–23 breeding pairs and occupied three to five separate colonies. The researchers also found that birds from other reintroduction sites and natural populations in places including Serbia and Croatia were visiting the area, making the park part of a wider Balkan Griffon Vulture population.The study concluded that the reintroduction had successfully established a new breeding nucleus in the park. However, the researchers stressed that the population was still vulnerable, particularly to accidental poisoning. They recommended continuing supplementary feeding and adaptive management while monitoring the population. The species therefore represents not the end of the conservation effort, but the completion of its initial establishment phase.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: England found 238 constituencies where at least 20% of properties are more than a 15-minute walk from green or blue spaces
articles.summary: UK News: Access to nature remains uneven across England, with hundreds of communities lacking convenient routes to green or blue spaces. New analysis by The Wi.
articles.body: Access to nature remains uneven across England, with hundreds of communities lacking convenient routes to green or blue spaces. New analysis by The Wildlife Trusts and Liberal Democrats for Nature and Climate found that 238 parliamentary constituencies, 44% of those in England, have at least 20% of properties located more than a 15-minute walk from an accessible green or blue space. The findings come as the Wildlife Trusts calls for greater action to improve access to parks, rivers, gardens and other natural areas. These findings underscore the growing calls for policymakers to prioritise equitable green space access as a fundamental component of public health and environmental planning across England.238 English constituencies have limited access to natureThe analysis examined Defra data and applied it to Westminster constituency boundaries to assess how easily people can reach accessible green and blue spaces. The Wildlife Trusts defines low access as having at least 20% of properties more than a 15-minute walk from such a space. The results identified 238 constituencies meeting that threshold, equivalent to 44% of all English parliamentary constituencies. Some of the largest concentrations are in urban areas, with London accounting for 50 of the constituencies, followed by the South East with 42 and the North West with 28. Harrow West, Croydon West and Nottingham East were among the constituencies with the lowest levels of access according to the analysis.The figures do not mean that every resident in these constituencies lacks access to nature. Rather, they identify areas where a significant proportion of properties are beyond the 15-minute walking threshold used in the analysis.Nature access varies alongside economic deprivationThe Wildlife Trusts' analysis also found a relationship between economic deprivation and limited access to nature. Seven of England's 10 most economically deprived constituencies appeared on its list of places with low access to green or blue spaces. Bradford West, Bradford East and Birmingham Perry Barr were among the examples identified in the analysis. The organisation argues that communities facing economic deprivation can also have fewer opportunities to benefit from nearby parks, rivers and other natural areas.The issue is not restricted to large cities. The Wildlife Trusts points to constituencies such as South Norfolk and mid-Leicestershire, where some residents can live in predominantly rural areas while still having limited access to public parks, footpaths or other usable natural spaces. This illustrates the difference between living in a rural constituency and having convenient, publicly accessible nature nearby.Green and blue spaces can also provide relief during heatThe findings have emerged after a summer of extreme heat across England, when some urban areas recorded temperatures above 38C. The Wildlife Trusts says parks, trees, rivers and other nature-rich spaces can provide cooler environments during periods of high temperatures. The organisation has also gathered public experiences of accessing nature during heatwaves. Its consultation included people describing local woods and other natural spaces as places where they could find shade, cooler air and opportunities for walking.The Wildlife Trusts' head of health and education, Dom Higgins, told The Guardian access to nearby natural spaces is particularly relevant as extreme weather events become more significant for public health. The charity points to evidence linking nature-rich environments with physical and mental health benefits, while stressing that these opportunities are not distributed equally.Wildlife Trusts calls for changes to improve accessThe Wildlife Trusts has set out proposals for improving access to green and blue spaces. The organisation says the proposals are intended to support the government's existing commitment to ensuring people can reach nature within a 15-minute walk. Among its proposals are making it easier for local authorities to acquire land for parks and green spaces, helping community groups buy land, and providing longer-term funding for the maintenance of public parks and gardens. It also wants access to nature to be considered more closely in housing and development planning, including requirements for climate- and nature-friendly developments.The charity has additionally called for improved access to major rivers, particularly in urban areas, and for community-led walking and cycling routes to be easier to establish. Its earlier analysis argues that new housing should increase, rather than reduce, access to nearby green space. The research therefore highlights a geographical dimension to access to nature: proximity alone does not guarantee that people can easily reach or use natural spaces. The Wildlife Trusts is now urging policymakers to use the data alongside local knowledge and public experiences when considering how England's parks, waterways and other green spaces should be planned and maintained.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: BENGALURU: Investigation into the abduction of a 21-year-old woman by a group of men from Rajasthan has taken a different turn, with police finding that the men allegedly acted on the instructions of her in-laws. The incident led to high drama on Magadi Road after alert members of the public chased and caught the abductors.In-laws allegedly wanted her back in RajasthanIn her complaint filed at Magadi Road police station, the woman alleged that her mother-in-law had threatened her with dire consequences if she did not leave her son, who lives in Agrahara Dasarahalli, and return to Rajasthan with the men sent to take her. She also alleged that the men misbehaved with her while forcing her into their Hyundai Venue on Wednesday evening.The incident went viral after the car driver rammed into several vehicles and injured a few people, including a nine-year-old girl, while fleeing. Video clips of members of the public chasing the car and thrashing its occupants also went viral. The public learnt of the alleged abduction when the woman told them she had married a man from another caste and was being forcibly taken back to Rajasthan.Couple married despite family oppositionMeanwhile, the woman’s husband, Ramesh (name changed), told police that their families had opposed their relationship, forcing the couple to opt for a court marriage in February. Citing a threat to their lives, Ramesh brought his wife to Bengaluru, where he has been working and living for over a decade.The couple initially stayed at a close relative’s house and recently moved into a newly constructed house on the second floor of a rented residential building.Three men allegedly kept watch on husbandBased on the woman’s complaint, Magadi Road police arrested Rakesh, 31, Karan, 28, and Ayan, 18, all from Pali in Rajasthan. Police said the trio had been hired by the woman’s father-in-law.They drove to Bengaluru around 10 days ago and stayed at a hotel near Majestic. They also allegedly monitored Ramesh’s movements by parking their vehicle some distance from his house. The car’s driver, identified as Saddam, remains at large.A senior police officer said Ramesh’s parents would also be arrested for their alleged role in planning and executing the abduction.Men allegedly used father’s name to lure her outAccording to cops, the men knocked on the woman’s door, claiming they had been sent by her father. Trusting them, she opened the door and walked with them to the car.She realised she had been trapped only when they made a video call to Ramesh’s mother.In her complaint, the woman said the abductors instructed Saddam to “mow down” anyone who came in their way.“The vehicle was being driven rashly and brushed against other vehicles on the road. articles.title: Abandoned pony limping through Kharagpur traffic rescued for veterinary care
articles.summary: KHARAGPUR: A 7- to 8-year-old skewbald pony found limping through traffic on Kharagpur’s Malancha Road with severely overgrown hooves and other painfu.
articles.body: KHARAGPUR: A 7- to 8-year-old skewbald pony found limping through traffic on Kharagpur’s Malancha Road with severely overgrown hooves and other painful health conditions has been rescued and transported to an Animal Rahat sanctuary for veterinary care and rehabilitation. The rescue was carried out following action by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals India (PETA India), with assistance from West Midnapore district magistrate Bijin Krishna; Superintendent of Police Papiya Sultana; Kharagpur sub-divisional officer Bhuvana Pranith Pappula; Kharagpur Animal Resources Development department deputy director Chinmoy Chakraborty; Kharagpur Town Police Station inspector-in charge Amit Kumar Mitra; and local animal advocate Sudebi Bhattacharya. The operation also received support from Members of Parliament June Maliah and Sayani Ghosh.The abandoned pony was suffering from severely overgrown and enlarged hooves, swollen fetlock joints, chronic osteoarthritis, and impaired mobility. Despite the animal’s evident distress, PETA India personnel faced resistance from certain locals, delaying rescue efforts. The pony was finally secured and taken for treatment after intervention by local authorities and the MPs.“This abandoned pony is yet another victim of the joyride industry. This rescue shows what can be achieved when authorities, animal protection groups, and citizens act together,” said Maliah. “I thank PETA India for never giving up on this pony and Animal Rahat for housing the pony and all the officials led by DM Bijin Krishna and SP Sultana for their prompt intervention in the rescue operation. I urge the public to help other ponies by choosing animal-free forms of entertainment.”In Kolkata, PETA India continues to campaign for the protection of horses used to haul tourist carriages. In June 2026 alone, the group registered three FIRs involving neglected or distressed horses, including a foal found running frantically through active traffic, a horse with severely overgrown hooves rescued from the Hastings area, and a mare who died in the middle of traffic in Ekbalpore. Since 2024, at least 18 horses in the city have reportedly died or succumbed to injuries from road accidents and other causes.The Calcutta High Court has taken note of the poor condition of horses, the prevalence of unlicensed hackney carriages, and the abandonment of ailing animals. In an order dated May 9, 2024, it directed the state government to develop a proposal to rehabilitate horse-carriage owners so that replacing horse-drawn carriages, as done in Mumbai, can be considered. On July 7, 2026, PETA India appealed for horse-drawn tourist carriages in Kolkata to be replaced with heritage-style electric carriages.PETA India, whose motto reads in part that “animals are not ours to use for entertainment,” opposes speciesism, a human-supremacist worldview.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.body: Tenant police verification is one of those legal requirements that many homeowners tend to overlook, often because the process traditionally meant standing in long queues at local police stations. Yet, ignoring it can have serious consequences. Under Section 188 of the IPC, failing to register tenant details can invite legal penalties, leaving property owners vulnerable to liability if their tenants misuse the premises. With states now offering online verification portals, the process has become far simpler and more accessible. Homeowners can protect themselves legally, ensure tenant records are properly logged, and avoid unnecessary visits to police stations—all from the comfort of their homes. This digital convenience not only saves time but also provides peace of mind, making compliance effortless and secure.What it solvesOnline tenant verification helps homeowners maintain security and legal compliance while saving time. It prevents misuse of property and ensures that tenant records are officially logged with the local police department.What to doSubmit your tenant’s details and ID proofs through your state’s official police web portal or citizen service site.Steps•Visit your state police website or citizen portal.•Create an account and select the “Tenant Verification” option.•Enter property owner and tenant details including full names and contact information.•Upload tenant photo, Aadhaar, and lease agreement signed by both parties.•Submit the application to receive an online acknowledgement receipt.NoteTenant verification is mandatory in many Indian states. articles.title: After Jantar Mantar setback, AIMPLB plans 3-month national UCC campaign, to take battle to states
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The All India Muslim Personal Law Board (AIMPLB) on Thursday postponed its proposed dharna against the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) at Jantar M.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The All India Muslim Personal Law Board (AIMPLB) on Thursday postponed its proposed dharna against the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) at Jantar Mantar after Delhi Police denied permission, citing the "likelihood of a large gathering and difficulty in managing the crowd".The Board said it had assured authorities that the demonstration would be peaceful and described assembly and protest as constitutional rights. AIMPLB spokesperson S Q R Ilyas, however, advised supporters planning to travel to Delhi not to proceed, asking them to avoid inconvenience and maintain peace.The demonstration was planned to mark the Delhi launch of the Board's three-month 'Save India, Save Sharia' campaign, also described as its 'Movement for Protection of Constitution and Sharia', to mobilise public opinion on constitutional rights, religious freedom and Muslim personal law.At an "emergency" press conference, president Maulana Khalid Saifullah Rahmani, spokesperson Dr Syed Qasim Rasool Ilyas and general secretary Maulana Mohd Fazlur Rahim Mujaddidi criticised the denial and said the campaign would continue through other democratic and legal means. The Board plans to hold public-awareness programmes and legal conventions in Hyderabad, Mumbai, Kolkata and Bengaluru, besides reaching out to religious leaders of other faiths, civil rights groups and tribal communities.The Board has already taken its opposition to the UCC and Waqf law to court. After Uttarakhand notified its UCC on January 27, 2025, AIMPLB filed a challenge in the Uttarakhand High Court in February. After the Gujarat Assembly passed its UCC Bill in March 2026, the Board announced in April that it would challenge the legislation in the Gujarat High Court.Separately, AIMPLB moved the Supreme Court against the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, filing its petition in April 2025. The plea challenges the amendments on constitutional grounds, including Articles 14, 25 and 26 — the Right to Equality, Freedom of Religion (Individual), and Freedom to Manage Religious Affairs (Group).The Board also announced a comprehensive 'White Paper' documenting what it describes as "discrimination against minorities and violations of constitutional and religious freedoms", besides setting out its legal objections to the Waqf law. Its proposed charter will cover the UCC, religious freedom, protection of waqf properties and religious places, hate crimes, alleged unlawful demolitions and equal enforcement of law. It is to be submitted to President Droupadi Murmu, seeking protection of minority rights under Articles 25 to 30.The police decision came amid renewed scrutiny of restrictions on protests at Jantar Mantar. On Thursday, the Delhi High Court questioned the police over its refusal to allow another proposed protest at the venue and asked how a blanket ban on demonstrations could be justified. articles.body: HYDERABAD: The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) objected to the proposed screening of a documentary on jailed activist Umar Khalid at IIIT-Hyderabad, saying screening an uncertified film would violate the Cinematograph Act unless an exemption had been granted, according to news agency PTI reported.The documentary, "Prisoner No. 626710 is Present", directed by filmmaker Lalit Vachani, was proposed to be screened by a group of students at the institute's KRB Auditorium at 8 pm on Friday. Sources said the students have now decided to cancel the screening."Public screening of a documentary film that has not yet been certified by the CBFC is a violation of the Cinematograph Act unless a specific exemption has been sought under the Act," the CBFC posted on X.Tagging IIIT-Hyderabad, the CBFC said the institute's authorities "may take note for necessary action".The CBFC functions under the Union Information and Broadcasting Ministry.IIIT-H, however, distanced itself from the proposed screening, saying neither the institute nor any of its recognised student bodies had organised or organised or hosted any screening of any film uncertified by the Central Board of Film Certification"."IIIT Hyderabad has established processes governing official events and activities on campus, and any claim attributing an unauthorised or unrelated activity to the Institute or its recognised student bodies is factually incorrect," it said.The institute said students and faculty from its large and diverse community may meet or interact with people in their individual capacities."Such personal interactions or visits, where they occur, should not be construed as Institute-organised events, articles.title: Calcutta HC orders CWC to return 3-year-old to couple despite adoption procedure not being followed
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: The Calcutta high court has directed a Child Welfare Committee to return a three-year-old child to the couple who had been caring for him s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Calcutta high court has directed a Child Welfare Committee to return a three-year-old child to the couple who had been caring for him since birth, holding that the committee had no legal basis to take custody of the child. The court in a judgment delivered on September 17, 2026, also directed the couple to approach the appropriate court to establish their legal status as the child’s adoptive parents.Why did the Child Welfare Committee take custody of the child?According to the court order, the child was born prematurely in February 2023 at M R Bangur Hospital, Kolkata. He was born at around 29 weeks and weighed about 1.68 kg. He remained in the hospital’s special newborn care unit for about 25 days.The child’s biological parents handed him over to the petitioners on the day he was discharged from hospital. The couple then cared for him and a notarised adoption deed was executed between them and the biological parents in April 2023.In February 2026, the couple approached the Child Welfare Committee after hospital authorities told them to approach the committee for adoption-related formalities before obtaining the child’s birth certificate. The committee took custody of the child and did not return him to the couple.What did the couple tell the high court?The couple said they had been looking after the child since he was born and there were no allegations that they had abused, neglected or harmed him. They argued that they had approached the committee only to complete the required formalities and should have been guided through the adoption process instead of losing custody of the child.The State, however, said the adoption had not followed the procedure required under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and the Adoption Regulations, 2022. It said a private adoption deed could not replace the legal process.What did the high court find?Justice Krishna Rao agreed that the proper adoption procedure had not been followed. It noted that the child was neither an orphan nor an abandoned child. It also found that the child did not fall within the legal category of a “child in need of care and protection”.The court explained that the Juvenile Justice Act gives the Child Welfare Committee powers to deal with children who fall within that category. It said the committee could not use those powers in a case where the child did not meet the legal definition.“There is no dispute that biological parents have given the child in adoption to the present petitioners without following the proper procedure. Admittedly, the child is neither “orphan” nor “abandoned”. The petitioners have accepted the child and decided to take care of the child by obtaining custody of the child from the biological parents. The Deed of Adoption executed between the parties is a notarized document. As per the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, merely by executing the notarized Adoption Deed, the petitioners cannot claim that they have right to hold the custody of the child. On the other hand, the Child Welfare Committee does not get any power to deal with the child who is neither “abandoned” nor “orphan”. The child involved in the present case also does not fall in the category of ‘children in need of care and protection’,” the court said.The court also considered the child’s welfare and the fact that he had been living with the couple since infancy. Section 3 of the Juvenile Justice Act lays down principles for dealing with children, including that their best interests, safety and family care should be given primary consideration.“For the ends of justice, it would be appropriate to direct the Child Welfare Committee to return of child to the petitioners. This is by the following the principle of the best interest of the child, principle of family responsibility, principle of safety, positive measures, principle of institutionalization as a measure of last resort, principle of repatriation and restoration, which are also enunciated as general principles in Section 3 of the Act of 2015,” it added.The court therefore held that the committee’s decision to take custody of the child was not in accordance with law because the child did not fall within the category of children who could be dealt with by the committee under the Act.“As the child is neither “orphan” nor “abandoned” and does not fall in the category of ‘children in need of care and protection’ in terms of Section 2(14) of the Act of 2015, the action of the Child Welfare Committee taking the custody of the child from the petitioners is not is accordance with law,” the court further observed.The high court directed the Child Welfare Committee to hand over the child to the couple by 4 pm on September 18, 2026. It also directed the District Legal Services Committee to seek quarterly reports on the child’s welfare and progress from December 2026.At the same time, the court made clear that the adoption process had not been legally completed. It directed the couple to approach the appropriate court for a declaration that they are the child’s adoptive parents.

articles.title: In 2007, a Florida hunger-relief group began packing meals for families in need; nearly two decades later, volunteers have packed more than 100 million meals
articles.summary: US News: In 2007, a small hunger-relief effort in Southwest Florida began with a simple idea: bring people together to pack nutritious meals for communities fa.
articles.body: In 2007, a small hunger-relief effort in Southwest Florida began with a simple idea: bring people together to pack nutritious meals for communities facing food insecurity. Nearly two decades later, Meals of Hope has grown into a major nonprofit operation, with volunteers packing more than 100 million meals for families in need across the United States and around the world. The milestone, reported by the Naples Daily News through Yahoo News, reflects years of community events involving schools, churches, businesses, civic groups and families. What began as a local response to hunger has become a volunteer-powered movement that combines practical help with a sense of shared purpose. Each sealed meal represents more than food in a box. It represents the time, care and cooperation of people determined to help their neighbours.A local idea grows into a national effortMeals of Hope began in Collier County, Florida, after founder Stephen Popper learned about children in Haiti who were struggling to learn because they did not have enough food.The story stayed with him. Instead of treating hunger as a distant problem, Popper and his supporters looked for a way to involve ordinary people directly. Their answer was a meal-packing event that allowed volunteers to work together, prepare food and see the immediate result of their efforts.The organisation held its first event in August 2007 with support from the Rotary Club of Naples. Around 500 volunteers packed more than 135,000 meals during that first event. The meals were donated to Haiti and the Harry Chapin Food Bank.The early success encouraged the group to continue. Meals of Hope soon established a larger goal of helping people both locally and internationally. The programme developed into a model that could be repeated in schools, workplaces, churches, community centres and other gathering places.Over time, the scale of the work changed dramatically. A project that began with a single event in Florida eventually involved thousands of volunteers and meal-packing events across the country.How a meal-packing event worksMeal-packing events are designed to be straightforward enough for people of different ages and backgrounds to join.Volunteers typically stand along assembly lines and work in groups. Some measure ingredients, while others fill bags, seal packets, label packages or place finished meals into boxes. The process is organised, but it is also social. Participants often work alongside people they have never met, united by a common goal.The meals are generally made from shelf-stable ingredients and prepared to provide essential nutrition. Once packed, they are sent to food banks, pantries and community organisations that distribute them to families and individuals facing hunger.The format allows a large number of people to contribute within a short time. It also makes hunger relief visible. Volunteers do not simply make a donation and walk away. They take part in the physical work of preparing food and can see how many meals their group has completed.For children and teenagers, the events can be an introduction to community service. For employers, they provide a way for staff members to volunteer together. Churches, schools and civic organisations can use them to turn a shared concern about hunger into practical action.More than 100 million mealsMeals of Hope says its volunteers have packed more than 100 million meals since the organisation was founded. The meals have been donated to communities across the United States and in other countries.The figure is difficult to picture. One hundred million meals would fill an enormous number of boxes, but the real meaning of the milestone lies in the number of people who may have received assistance through the organisation’s network.Food insecurity can affect people for many different reasons. A family may face a sudden job loss, high housing costs, a medical bill, a natural disaster or a period of reduced income. Older adults, children and people living alone may also struggle to afford enough food.Food banks and pantries help fill the gap. They provide groceries and prepared food when household budgets cannot stretch far enough. Meal-packing programmes add another supply of shelf-stable food that can be stored and distributed when it is needed.The 100 million meal milestone also represents millions of volunteer hours. Behind each meal are people who measured ingredients, sealed packets, lifted boxes, organised events and helped move food into local communities.The importance of local food supportAlthough Meals of Hope operates across the country and internationally, its roots remain in Southwest Florida.The organisation operates food pantries in the region and continues to support local hunger-relief efforts. Its work has expanded beyond occasional meal-packing events to include regular food distribution and pantry services.That local focus matters because hunger is not always easy to see. It can exist in neighbourhoods with busy shopping areas, new homes and growing businesses. Families may be working but still unable to afford enough food after paying for rent, transportation, childcare and utilities.Local food banks understand the communities they serve. They work with schools, charities, shelters and other organisations that can identify families who need support. National meal-packing efforts become more effective when the food reaches groups with established local networks.Food distribution also requires careful planning. Meals must be transported, stored and delivered safely. Volunteers and partner organisations help connect the packed food with people who need it.Volunteers are at the centreThe organisation’s growth has depended on community participation. Meals of Hope events attract volunteers from different generations and backgrounds, including employees, students, families, faith groups and service organisations.That broad participation has helped meal packing become more than a charity activity. It has become a shared community experience.A volunteer may spend only a few hours at an event, but those hours become part of a much larger effort. When hundreds of people work at the same time, they can prepare tens of thousands of meals in a single day.The group’s website says volunteers have helped provide more than 100 million meals to date. Other reports have placed the organisation’s total even higher as more recent events have continued. The exact figure may change as new meals are packed, but the larger message remains the same: repeated local actions can create a substantial long-term impact.For many participants, the experience can also change how they think about hunger. Working directly with food and learning where it will go can make food insecurity feel less abstract.A model built on cooperationMeals of Hope’s approach relies on cooperation between the nonprofit, volunteers, donors and distribution partners.Donations help pay for ingredients, packaging, equipment, transport and event coordination. Volunteers provide the labour. Food banks and pantries handle distribution. Schools, businesses and community groups often help recruit participants and host events.Each part of the process is necessary. Packed meals are useful only when they can reach communities safely and efficiently. Distribution partners understand local needs and can direct food to families, shelters and organisations that require it.This structure also allows the programme to respond to different circumstances. Meal-packing events can support routine food assistance, but they can also provide supplies after disasters or during periods when food banks experience unusually high demand.The model is simple enough to repeat and flexible enough to work in different locations. That may be one reason it has continued to grow over nearly 20 years.The work is not finishedThe 100 million meal milestone is a significant achievement, but it does not mean the problem of hunger has been solved.Food insecurity continues to affect communities throughout Florida, the wider United States and other parts of the world. Food prices, housing costs and emergencies can quickly increase the number of people seeking help.Meal-packing organisations are one part of the hunger-relief system. They work alongside food banks, government programmes, schools, community kitchens and local charities. Long-term progress also requires attention to wages, housing, healthcare and access to affordable food.Still, the availability of nutritious meals can make an immediate difference. A food box can help a parent prepare dinner, support a child during a difficult week or give an older adult food to rely on until the next income payment arrives.That immediate assistance is why volunteers continue to participate.A milestone made of many small effortsThe history of Meals of Hope shows how a modest local initiative can develop into a far-reaching movement.In 2007, volunteers gathered in Florida to pack meals inspired by a concern about hungry children. Nearly 20 years later, more than 100 million meals have been packed and donated to communities in need.The achievement belongs to the organisation, but also to the people who have taken part in the work. It includes the volunteer who attended one event, the school that organised an annual packing day, the company that brought its employees together and the food bank that distributed the finished meals.Each individual contribution may have seemed small. Together, those contributions created a supply of food large enough to reach families across regions and borders.The story is a reminder that meaningful change does not always begin with a grand plan. articles.title: Yellow-bellied venomous sea snake returns to California beach after 8 years; rare reappearance after 2018 gives scientists clues about the species’ changing Pacific range
articles.summary: US News: A yellow-bellied sea snake has washed ashore on an Orange County beach, marking the first reported appearance of the venomous species in California si.
articles.body: A yellow-bellied sea snake has washed ashore on an Orange County beach, marking the first reported appearance of the venomous species in California since 2018. The rare sighting took place at Crystal Cove, according to video footage cited by the Los Angeles Times. The snake’s return has drawn attention from scientists because these ocean-dwelling reptiles are rarely seen so far north. Experts believe warm Pacific waters and shifting ocean currents may help explain how the animal reached Southern California. Although the snake carries potent venom, it is not considered a danger to people who leave it alone. Researchers are now hoping to verify the sighting and learn whether the appearance reflects an isolated event or a broader change in the species’ Pacific range.A rare visitor returnsThe yellow-bellied sea snake is an unusual sight on any California beach. The species spends its entire life in the ocean, where it hunts fish and moves with the help of currents. It is far more commonly associated with tropical and subtropical waters than with the cooler coastline of Southern California.That is why the recent appearance at Crystal Cove has attracted scientific interest. The snake was filmed on the beach at night, where a person appeared to use the base of a palm frond to move it back towards the water. The footage was broadcast by CBS Los Angeles and later reported by the Los Angeles Times.The sighting is the first reported California appearance since 2018, when two yellow-bellied sea snakes were seen in Orange County. Since 1972, there have been only six confirmed sightings in the state, according to Greg Pauly, a reptile expert with the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County.For a species that normally remains offshore and is rarely encountered by people, every confirmed record can provide useful information.Why the snake reached CaliforniaScientists believe ocean conditions may have played a role in the snake’s arrival.Yellow-bellied sea snakes hunt in open water and can be carried by currents. If warm water moves northward, the animals may travel farther from their usual range without immediately experiencing temperatures that are uncomfortable.Hayley Crowell, a snake expert at San Diego State University, said the recent sighting may be linked to warm ocean water during the summer. She explained that the snakes can be swept off course by currents and may not recognise that they have moved far from their normal habitat if the water remains warm enough.The Pacific Ocean is constantly changing. Seasonal weather patterns, ocean circulation and climate-related warming can influence where marine animals are found. Species that normally remain in warmer regions may occasionally appear farther north when conditions allow.That does not mean every unusual sighting signals a permanent expansion of a species’ range. A single animal may simply have been carried away from its usual habitat. Scientists need repeated observations, verified photographs and environmental data before they can determine whether a lasting shift is occurring.The yellow-bellied sea snakeThe snake gets its name from the bright yellow underside that contrasts with its darker upper body. That striking pattern can make the animal easier to recognise in photographs, although identifying a sea snake from unclear footage can still be difficult.Yellow-bellied sea snakes belong to a group of roughly 65 to 75 species known as true sea snakes. Unlike sea kraits, which may leave the water to rest or lay eggs, true sea snakes are completely adapted to ocean life. They give birth to live young in the water and do not need to come ashore as part of their normal life cycle.Their flattened, paddle-like tails help them swim, while their bodies allow them to move efficiently through open water. The snakes use venom to subdue fish, which make up their diet.Although their venom is powerful, yellow-bellied sea snakes do not normally pose a threat to beachgoers. They are not interested in attacking people, and humans do not resemble their usual prey.The main risk arises when someone attempts to pick up, touch or restrain one.Experts warn people not to handle itThe snake seen at Crystal Cove appeared helpless on the beach. Because yellow-bellied sea snakes are built for swimming, they cannot move effectively on land. Their bodies may flop or twist as they try to return to the water, which can make them appear distressed.That helpless appearance may tempt people to intervene. However, experts say members of the public should avoid handling a sea snake, even if they believe they are trying to help.Crowell said people who do not handle the animal are generally safe. She also advised calling wildlife officials for assistance rather than attempting to move the snake themselves.Sea snakes may bite when they feel threatened or trapped.
